props.title: Long Weekend
props.initialSlug: Nature turns deadly against campers in Outback hell

sections.content: Long Weekend stands as one of Australian cinema's most unsettling ecological horror films. Director Colin Eggleston crafts a haunting tale of nature's revenge that influenced later eco-horror like The Birds (1963) and Phenomena (1985). The film's brutal portrayal of a toxic relationship against environmental devastation creates suffocating tension, while its subtle supernatural elements blur the line between psychological breakdown and natural retribution. Like Picnic at Hanging Rock (1975), it taps into Australia's cultural anxiety about its vast, untamed wilderness.

sections.content: The late 1970s marked a golden age for Australian eco-horror, with films like Mad Max (1979) and The Last Wave (1977) exploring humanity's fraught relationship with the environment. Long Weekend distinguishes itself through intimate scale and mounting dread rather than spectacle. The film's influence echoes in later works like In the Earth (2021) and Annihilation (2018), where nature becomes an incomprehensible, hostile force.

Eggleston's direction emphasizes the landscape as a character, similar to Nicolas Roeg's approach in Walkabout (1971). The film's sound design remains groundbreaking - natural sounds become increasingly threatening, creating an atmosphere that influenced The Blair Witch Project (1999) and The Ritual (2017). Its eco-horror themes feel especially relevant today, predating similar environmental warnings in films like The Day After Tomorrow (2004). SUBHEAD: Environmental Horror Evolution

sections.content: Long Weekend helped establish tropes that would define eco-horror for decades. Its influence can be seen in films like The Ruins (2008) and The Beach House (2019), where nature becomes an active, malevolent force rather than passive backdrop. The film's approach to environmental revenge particularly resonates with Japanese horror like Godzilla (1954) and modern eco-thrillers like The Host (2006).
